titre: The 1913 Armory Show, Founding Scandal of American Modern Art
accroche: In 1913, New York mocks Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase. In Chicago, the scandal arrives before the show does, and the crowds follow.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 17, 1913, the Association of American Painters and Sculptors opens the International Exhibition of Modern Art at the 69th Regiment Armory in New York: about thirteen hundred paintings, sculptures and decorative works by more than three hundred American and European artists, roughly a fifth of them women. Chaired by the painter Arthur B. Davies and organized by Walt Kuhn and Walter Pach, the show introduces an American public used to realistic art to Impressionist, Fauvist and Cubist works. The lawyer John Quinn, who gives the opening speech, had persuaded Congress to lift the customs duty on foreign works of art less than twenty years old. The organizers want noise: they have halftone postcards printed of fifty-seven works, and their posters advertise Matisse, Brancusi, Van Gogh and Cézanne, the last two dead since 1890 and 1906.

## The Painting No One Can See

Among the works on view, one canvas becomes the most notorious: *Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2*, painted the year before by the Frenchman Marcel Duchamp. Visitors look for the nude figure promised by the title and find only a sequence of planes; in Chicago, a critic even gives a very serious lecture trying to pinpoint the woman in the picture. The New York Tribune calls the show "remarkable, despite some freakish absurdities." The most quoted line, "an explosion in a shingle factory," is attributed sometimes to the critic Julian Street, sometimes to the essayist Joel Spingarn: even the origin of the show's most famous jibe is not firmly established. The writer J. F. Griswold publishes a parody of it in the New York Evening Sun, titled *The Rude Descending a Staircase (Rush Hour at the Subway)*. The painting finds a buyer all the same, during the show: Frederic C. Torrey of San Francisco.

## Ridicule as Publicity

The exhibition then travels to the Art Institute of Chicago, where it is cut to 634 works for lack of space, and on to the Copley Society of Art in Boston, where the American works are removed for the same reason. In Chicago, a Chicago Tribune editorial accuses the nudes of blurring the line between the artistic and the obscene, and the scandal reaches the governor of Illinois. In twenty-three days, 188,560 people come to see the show, more than in New York, roughly eight percent of the city's population at the time. According to the Illinois State Museum, its reputation for scandal had preceded it and may have softened some of the angriest reactions.

None of this is an accident. Mary Savig, a specialist at the Archives of American Art, points out that the organizers wanted the show to be sensational: they hoped for headlines that would push the public to go and see for themselves. Ridicule does not hurt the exhibition, then, it works for it. Quinn had said as much at the opening: it was time for the American people to have the chance to see and judge for themselves the work of the Europeans who are creating a new art. What remains to be asked is what the Chicago crowds came to judge: the art, or the scandal.

quiz.question: Why does Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 become the most mocked canvas of the 1913 Armory Show?
choix: Because it is the only Cubist work in the show, the others being Impressionist
Because the organizers refused to circulate its image, which keeps up the mystery
Because Duchamp is the only European artist invited to New York
Because the public searches in vain for the nude figure promised by the title, and the press mocks it
quiz.explication: Visitors and critics look for the woman in the title without finding her, and the press mocks it. The show nevertheless brought together Impressionist, Fauvist and Cubist works by more than three hundred European and American artists, and the organizers had postcards printed of fifty-seven works, this nude among them.
